criteria.name: Mission concept and rationale — What will it do, who are the users, why is it needed?
criteria.reasoning: The rationale for reef monitoring is clear and footnoted, and the main users (marine and conservation scientists) are identified. Mission objectives are vague ('could also be used'), with no quantitative requirements such as resolution, revisit or coverage. Users beyond scientists (reef managers, tourism operators) are not developed. The stated orbit contradicts the mission goal, weakening the requirements picture. Referencing is URL footnotes rather than a reference list.

evidence.quote: A near-real-time relay to monitoring stations on the ground would allow marine and conservation scientists
Hundreds of millions of humans rely on reefs for food, natural protection, jobs, and tourism.
My current choice is a geostationary orbit at an altitude of 600 km, which keeps the satellite fixed above the reef at all times.

criteria.name: Project plan — How you plan to complete the assignment, including either a Gantt chart or a timetable and information sources you plan to use
criteria.reasoning: A Gantt chart with stages, status colours and deadlines gives a feasible plan. However, there are no explicit contingencies or variation provisions. The text says weeks 7 and 8 are for editing, but the chart places Editing & Finalisation in weeks 9 and 10. The plan is not tied to the mission narrative, and information sources are only implied rather than listed.

evidence.quote: Project work will be divided into weeks via a Gantt Chart.
Weeks 7 and 8 are reserved for review, amendments, final simulations, and reflection.

criteria.name: Preliminary progress — Technical content and evidence of sufficient work done to date
criteria.reasoning: Progress is limited to reading a brief, background research and completing tutorials. No preliminary calculations, orbit parameters, STK outputs or figures are presented, so no technical results are shown. The only design decision stated (GEO at 600 km) is technically incorrect. The work shown does not demonstrate that the project is on track.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Sections are clearly headed and the report reads reasonably well, with footnotes matched to superscripts. The Gantt chart has no figure caption or number and uses undefined grey and white cells. Some phrasing is awkward or informal ('maybe only one is required', 'More STK simulations needed'). The report lacks the software, information-sources and technical sections the brief asks for.

evidence.quote: Oceans have become 30 percent more acidic since the industrial revolution leading to the bleaching of coral reefs.

technical_issues.issue: A geostationary orbit is at about 35,786 km altitude over the equator, not 600 km. A 600 km orbit cannot remain fixed above the reef at 15–24°S, so the stated orbit is physically incorrect.
A single GEO relay is not justified for near-real-time monitoring of the reef at useful resolution. The chosen orbit is inconsistent with the stated mission goal and no trade-off is shown.

Ocean acidification is cited as the cause of bleaching, but bleaching is driven mainly by thermal stress. The 30% figure refers to a hydrogen-ion concentration increase and is not explained, so the causal link is overstated.
The text reserves weeks 7 and 8 for editing, but the Gantt chart schedules Editing & Finalisation in weeks 9 and 10. The schedule is internally inconsistent.
The bathymetry claim is attributed to 'current satellites' but cites a DeepReef depth model, which is not a satellite product. The source does not support the claim as worded.

overall: The report gives a sound reef-monitoring rationale and a usable Gantt chart, but it has no technical results and its central orbit choice (GEO at 600 km) is physically wrong. Software, information sources and contingencies are underdeveloped, and the schedule is inconsistent with the text.

feedback.summary: You have a clear case for reef monitoring, with footnoted sources and well-identified users in marine and conservation science. The main gaps are technical. The geostationary orbit at 600 km cannot hold the reef in view, so the design needs rethinking before progress can be judged. Your progress evidence is also thin: you have completed tutorials but no results yet. Addressing these points would strengthen the report considerably.
next_steps: Revisit your orbit choice. A geostationary orbit sits about 35,786 km above the equator, so a 600 km orbit cannot keep the reef in view. Select an orbit suited to near-real-time reef imaging, and include a brief trade-off between altitude, revisit time and resolution.

Make the schedule consistent: place editing in weeks 7 and 8 in both the text and the Gantt chart. Add contingencies for delays or STK problems, and correct the acidification and bathymetry claims so each statement matches its source.

Produce first STK results, such as orbit parameters, coverage or revisit calculations, with a short interpretation. Then add software and information-sources sections, with a reference list that matches your in-text citations.

criteria.C1: Your rationale is clear: reef monitoring is well motivated, you identify marine and conservation scientists as users, and you explain why reefs matter to people. To reach the Accomplished band, define quantitative objectives and requirements (resolution, revisit, coverage) and develop other users such as reef managers and tourism operators. Correct your orbit, bleaching and bathymetry claims, and turn your footnote URLs into a proper reference list.
criteria.C2: You have a feasible plan: the Gantt chart shows stages, status colours and deadlines. However, the text places editing in weeks 7 and 8 while the chart shows weeks 9 and 10, so these must be reconciled. To reach the Accomplished band, add explicit contingencies and variation provisions, tie the schedule to the mission narrative, and list your information sources with references.
criteria.C3: Your progress so far is mainly reading, background research and STK tutorials 1 to 4. No preliminary calculations, orbit parameters or STK outputs are presented, and your only design decision (GEO at 600 km) is technically incorrect. To reach at least the Adequate band, show initial results such as orbit calculations or coverage plots, with a short interpretation explaining what they mean for your mission.
criteria.C4: Your sections are clearly headed and the report reads reasonably well, with footnotes matched to superscripts. To improve, give the Gantt chart a numbered caption and define its colour coding. Remove informal phrasing such as 'maybe only one is required' and 'More STK simulations needed'.
